Vision
VIZH-un
n. (a revelatory sight granted by God to a prophet; rendering Hebrew chazon, mar'ah, Greek horama, optasia)
From Latin visio, a seeing, from videre, to see. The English word has drifted toward the man's own foresight or ambition; the biblical word is the reverse — something shown to a man who was not looking, by God who was.

Biblical Definition

A vision in Scripture is not a man's plan for the future but God's self-disclosure to a prophet, given while the prophet is awake and often against his expectation. The Lord defines the term Himself when Aaron and Miriam presume to speak as Moses' equals: “If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream” (Numbers 12:6). The vision is therefore a mode of revelation, ranked below the face-to-face speech granted to Moses but genuinely and objectively from God. Abram receives one: “the word of the LORD came unto Abram in a vision” (Genesis 15:1). Habakkuk is told to write his down and make it legible, because a vision is a message with content, not an experience with a mood: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Habakkuk 2:2). Where the word is absent, the covenant people are in famine — “the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision” (1 Samuel 3:1) — and this is the key to the most abused verse in the English Bible, Proverbs 29:18. Paul's summary of his own conversion sets the pattern for every man who has heard God speak: he was “not disobedient unto the heavenly vision” (Acts 26:19). A vision is not a thing to savour; it is a thing to obey.

Webster 1828 Definition

A revelatory sight given by God to a prophet while awake. Numbers 12:6 makes it the standard prophetic mode; Habakkuk 2:2 makes it a written, legible message; Proverbs 29:18 laments its absence, not the absence of human ambition.

expand to see more

VISION, n. s as z. [L. visio, from video, visus, to see.] The act of seeing external objects; actual sight.

2. The faculty of seeing; sight.

3. Something imagined to be seen, though not real; a phantom; an apparition.

4. In Scripture, a revelation from God; an appearance or exhibition of something supernaturally presented to the minds of the prophets, by which they were informed of future events. Such were the visions of Isaiah, Amos, Ezekiel.

5. Something imaginary; the production of fancy. Where there is no vision, the people perish. Prov. 29.

Key Scripture

Numbers 12:6 — "And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream."

Habakkuk 2:2 — "And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it."

1 Samuel 3:1 — "And the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli. And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision."

Proverbs 29:18 — "Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he."

Modern Corruption

Proverbs 29:18 has been lifted out of the Bible and made the motto of corporate strategy and church-growth seminars, where “vision” means the leader's ambition rather than God's revealed word — and the second half of the verse, which defines the first, is almost never quoted.

expand to see more

“Where there is no vision, the people perish” is very likely the most misappropriated half-verse in English. It is printed on leadership posters, quoted at board retreats, and preached to justify a pastor casting a five-year plan, on the assumption that vision means a compelling picture of a preferred future. The Hebrew word is chazon, the technical term for prophetic revelation — the same word that heads the books of Isaiah, Obadiah, and Nahum. The verse laments a nation with no prophetic word from God, exactly the famine described in 1 Samuel 3:1 and threatened in Amos 8:11. And Solomon supplies his own gloss in the same breath: “but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.” The antidote to no-vision is not strategic planning; it is the written law of God kept. To quote the first clause without the second is to invert the proverb into a charter for precisely the self-appointed leadership it condemns.

The second corruption is a charismatic one, and it runs in the opposite direction: the term is applied to impressions, mental pictures, and private experiences claimed as fresh revelation, with the canon left formally intact and practically supplemented. Numbers 12:6 sets vision alongside dream as the ordinary prophetic mode of the old covenant; Hebrews 1:1-2 announces that God, who spoke in those many modes, has now spoken in His Son. The dictionary holds the cessationist position of the Reformed confessions: the canon is closed, and the sufficiency of Scripture is not a claim about how much God could say but about how much He has said and bound us to. A man who has the whole written Word and still waits for a vision has not understood what he already holds in his hands.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chazon (prophetic revelation, from chazah, to see or gaze) and mar'ah (a sight, appearance); Greek horama (that which is seen) and optasia (an appearing).

expand to see more

Hebrew chazon (H2377) — prophetic revelation, oracle; the word that titles Isaiah 1:1, Obadiah 1, and Nahum 1:1, and the word in Proverbs 29:18.

Hebrew chazah (H2372) — to gaze, behold, see as a seer; the verb behind both chazon and chozeh (seer).

Hebrew mar'ah (H4759) — a sight or appearance; the word in Numbers 12:6 and in Ezekiel's visions of God.

Greek horama (G3705) — that which is seen, a spectacle or divinely granted sight; used of Peter's sheet and Paul's Macedonian call (Acts 10:17; 16:9).

Greek optasia (G3701) — an appearing, a vision granted; used in Luke 1:22, Acts 26:19, and 2 Corinthians 12:1.

Usage

"“There was no open vision” — the famine of the word of God, not a shortage of leadership imagination."

"“Write the vision, and make it plain” — a real vision has propositional content that can be written down and read at speed."

"“Not disobedient unto the heavenly vision” — the proper response to revelation is obedience, not repetition of the experience."
